foundation.label: Foundation Quiz
foundation.title: The AI gap is not a side plot. It is the reason this room exists.
foundation.intro: Answer fifteen foundation questions, then try the two bonus questions. The score is out of 15, but the extra credit girls can still get 17/15.

questions.prompt: Why does the AI gap between men and women matter for lAIdies?
options: Because AI is a personality test
Because confidence and access gaps can become power, pay, and influence gaps
Because the topic should be watered down
Because everyone should chase every tech trend
questions.answer: Because confidence and access gaps can become power, pay, and influence gaps
questions.explain: The point is not novelty. If one group gets fluent sooner, that group gets more say in how the work changes.
questions.review: Find it in the lAIdies positioning and About section.

questions.prompt: What is the lAIdies stance on women learning AI?
options: The references are the whole lesson
Smart professionals deserve accurate, practical AI learning that is also enjoyable and memorable
AI should stay with technical teams only
Learning AI is mostly about memorizing product names
questions.answer: Smart professionals deserve accurate, practical AI learning that is also enjoyable and memorable
questions.explain: The references are a memory and joy system. They do not replace substance, and they are not remedial packaging.
questions.review: Find it in the brand promise and About section.

questions.prompt: What happens if busy women wait until AI feels perfectly clear before trying it?
options: The gap quietly gets smaller by itself
Someone else builds the habits, vocabulary, and confidence first
AI stops changing work
The tools become risk-free
questions.answer: Someone else builds the habits, vocabulary, and confidence first
questions.explain: Waiting feels reasonable in a full calendar, but early comfort compounds into workplace advantage.
questions.review: Find it in the lAIdies purpose and Episode 1 starting point.

questions.prompt: Why is AI becoming part of the invisible load at work?
options: Because everyone is expected to magically know what to use, when to use it, and how to judge the output
Because AI only affects engineers
Because meetings got shorter
Because the tools explain office politics perfectly
questions.answer: Because everyone is expected to magically know what to use, when to use it, and how to judge the output
questions.explain: lAIdies exists because AI fluency is becoming another quiet expectation, and quiet expectations rarely land evenly.
questions.review: Find it in the Episode 1 working summary.

questions.prompt: When women learn AI, what changes besides individual productivity?
options: They can shape workflows, ask sharper questions, challenge weak outputs, and influence how AI gets used
They stop needing judgment
They become the office help desk by default
They should use AI to make every answer sound the same
questions.answer: They can shape workflows, ask sharper questions, challenge weak outputs, and influence how AI gets used
questions.explain: The larger goal is agency. Fluency helps women participate in decisions about the work, not just speed through tasks.
questions.review: Find it in the lAIdies purpose and community framing.

questions.prompt: What does lAIdies reject as the price of AI fluency?
options: Learning useful vocabulary
Trying low-risk tools
Having to become a totally different technical identity before participating
Keeping standards and judgment
questions.answer: Having to become a totally different technical identity before participating
questions.explain: The bar is not becoming someone else. The bar is enough fluency to use the tools, evaluate the output, and stay in the conversation.
questions.review: Find it in Episode 1 and the About section.

questions.prompt: Why does lAIdies make the first AI moves small?
options: Small moves make confidence real enough to repeat
Small moves mean the topic is not serious
Small moves avoid learning anything practical
Small moves are only for beginners forever
questions.answer: Small moves make confidence real enough to repeat
questions.explain: The confidence loop starts with usable experience: try, compare, notice what works, keep judgment, and try again.
questions.review: Find it in the Episode 1 Fun Pack Try-On.

questions.prompt: Why is community part of closing the AI gap?
options: Because private confusion becomes shared vocabulary, examples, receipts, and shortcuts
Because AI works only when discussed publicly
Because every question needs consensus
Because women should outsource judgment to the group
questions.answer: Because private confusion becomes shared vocabulary, examples, receipts, and shortcuts
questions.explain: A room changes the learning curve. People move faster when they can trade questions, warnings, examples, and wins.
questions.review: Find it in the community section.

questions.prompt: What must stay with the human as AI becomes more useful?
options: Judgment, standards, context, and accountability
Every first draft
A fear of clicking the wrong button
The belief that polished output is always right
questions.answer: Judgment, standards, context, and accountability
questions.explain: Fluency is not blind trust. It is knowing how to use help without handing over your name, standards, or responsibility.
questions.review: Find it in Episode 1's core lesson.

questions.prompt: What is one foundational reason lAIdies was created?
options: To make AI fluency practical, credible, and culturally alive for women before the gap gets wider
To make AI feel unserious
To replace source checking with confidence
To prove one AI tool is always best
questions.answer: To make AI fluency practical, credible, and culturally alive for women before the gap gets wider
questions.explain: The mission is practical fluency with taste and standards: useful enough for work, memorable enough to stick, and welcoming enough to start.
questions.review: Find it in the site promise and Episode 1.

questions.prompt: Why does starting now — instead of waiting until AI feels clearer — actually matter?
options: Because the tools will be discontinued soon
Because women are adopting AI less than men right now, and early comfort quietly compounds into a real workplace advantage
Because you have to be first or it is pointless
Because AI stops improving if you wait
questions.answer: Because women are adopting AI less than men right now, and early comfort quietly compounds into a real workplace advantage
questions.explain: The gap today is an adoption gap — fewer women are reaching for these tools. The fix is not talent; it is starting. Comfort built now compounds later.
questions.review: Find it in Episode 1's opening.

questions.prompt: What do you already have that makes you good at working with AI?
options: A computer science degree
A career's worth of judgment, communication, and taste — the skills AI cannot replicate
Nothing, until you learn to code
A perfect memory for product names
questions.answer: A career's worth of judgment, communication, and taste — the skills AI cannot replicate
questions.explain: The skills long dismissed as soft — briefing clearly, catching what is off, knowing what good looks like — turned out to be the hard ones. You have been training for this.
questions.review: Find it in Episode 2 and the About section.

questions.prompt: Why does lAIdies teach AI through a town — SUNNYVAiLE — instead of a plain how-to guide?
options: Because a how-to guide would be more accurate
Because a story you can walk around in makes the lessons stick, and gives you a reason to come back every week
Because AI can only be explained through fiction
Because the town is just decoration over the real lessons
questions.answer: Because a story you can walk around in makes the lessons stick, and gives you a reason to come back every week
questions.explain: You forget a listicle by lunch. You remember Cher, Elle, and a coffee order — and a place you actually want to revisit. Do not just learn from books; learn from hooks.
questions.review: Find it in the SUNNYVAiLE welcome and the town map.

questions.prompt: Why is SUNNYVAiLE frozen in 1999, full of the pop culture and gadgets of the era?
options: Because AI did not exist after 1999
Because a warm, familiar world takes the fear out of an intimidating topic and makes it fun to learn
Because older technology works better
Because the 90s had the best AI tools
questions.answer: Because a warm, familiar world takes the fear out of an intimidating topic and makes it fun to learn
questions.explain: AI can feel cold and intimidating. Wrapping it in something you already love — the mixtapes, the Dream Phone, the movies — makes it approachable instead of alienating.
questions.review: Find it in the SUNNYVAiLE welcome.

questions.prompt: What can you do in SUNNYVAiLE that you cannot get by googling how to use AI?
options: Nothing — it is the same information with a filter
Hand your real prompt to the Fairy Godmother and watch it get fixed, take the quiz, and learn with a crew — tools and a town, not just tips
Only read definitions
Buy a certificate
questions.answer: Hand your real prompt to the Fairy Godmother and watch it get fixed, take the quiz, and learn with a crew — tools and a town, not just tips
questions.explain: Anyone can google a prompt template. Only here can you hand over your real prompt, watch it get glowed up, and learn why — with people, every week.
questions.review: Find it at the FAiRY Godmother and around town.

questions.prompt: Bonus: why does representation in AI use and decision-making matter?
options: The people who use, question, and shape the tools influence what gets automated, trusted, funded, and normalized
Only engineers can shape AI outcomes
Representation matters only in marketing
The tools are neutral enough that workplace context does not matter
questions.answer: The people who use, question, and shape the tools influence what gets automated, trusted, funded, and normalized
questions.explain: AI adoption is not just personal productivity. It affects whose standards and assumptions get built into future workflows.
questions.review: Find it in the lAIdies purpose and community framing.

questions.prompt: Bonus: what happens when women build real AI fluency together?
options: They become harder to sideline in conversations about the future of work
They never need expert advice again
They should accept every AI answer faster
They turn every task into a tech project
questions.answer: They become harder to sideline in conversations about the future of work
questions.explain: Shared fluency changes posture: more questions, better standards, stronger participation, and less waiting for permission.
questions.review: Find it in the lAIdies mission and community framing.

issue01.label: Episode 01 Quiz
issue01.optionLabel: Episode 01: On Wednesdays We Use AI
issue01.title: Opening the tab without making it a whole personality crisis.
issue01.intro: Answer ten Episode 1 questions, then try the two bonus questions from next week's locker. A perfect 12/10 gets two stickers because we are not monsters.

questions.prompt: What is the actual first move in Episode 1?
options: Take a 40-hour course first
Open the tab and try one small thing
Wait until your company has a perfect AI strategy
Pretend Cher's closet computer never happened
questions.answer: Open the tab and try one small thing
questions.explain: Episode 1 is about starting small. Ten minutes beats waiting for a mythical free weekend.
questions.review: Find it in the opening and the Episode 1 Fun Pack Try-On.

questions.prompt: Why does AI feel urgent for busy corporate women?
options: Because everyone needs to become a developer
Because it is being added to the invisible load
Because meetings are too short
Because PowerPoint asked nicely
questions.answer: Because it is being added to the invisible load
questions.explain: The point is not chasing hype. The point is not letting another workplace expectation land on you without support.
questions.review: Find it in the Working Summary and the opening argument.

questions.prompt: lAIdies is not asking you to become:
options: More confident with useful tools
Curious in public
The IT department in better shoes
Someone who asks better questions
questions.answer: The IT department in better shoes
questions.explain: You can learn enough technical context to stop feeling locked out without turning into the help desk.
questions.review: Find it in the section about what lAIdies is and is not.

questions.prompt: What makes generative AI different from regular search?
options: It only finds old webpages
It refuses to draft
It can create a new first pass from your instructions
It always knows the truth
questions.answer: It can create a new first pass from your instructions
questions.explain: Episode 1 frames AI as something that can draft, summarize, compare, translate tone, and organize, not just search.
questions.review: Find it in the Core Lesson.

questions.prompt: What does Cher's closet computer prove?
options: Fashion is more important than work
AI only works with plaid
Useful technology can feel fun and practical
You need a Beverly Hills budget to start
questions.answer: Useful technology can feel fun and practical
questions.explain: The reference works because it makes the tech feel less sterile and more obviously useful.
questions.review: Find it in the reference discussion around Cher's closet.

questions.prompt: What does 'small sips, big moves' mean here?
options: Only learn AI at happy hour
Never read documentation
Try one manageable move instead of waiting to feel ready
Make every project tiny forever
questions.answer: Try one manageable move instead of waiting to feel ready
questions.explain: The series is meant to make AI practice small enough that people actually do it.
questions.review: Find it in the Episode 1 Fun Pack Try-On and Episode promise.

questions.prompt: Why does Episode 1 ask you to try the same prompt in ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini?
options: To see which tool feels most useful for the same low-risk task
To prove one tool is always best
To memorize three product pages
To make the evening disappear
questions.answer: To see which tool feels most useful for the same low-risk task
questions.explain: Same ask, different tools, better comparison. It is a try-on, not a final exam.
questions.review: Find it in the Episode 1 Fun Pack Try-On.

questions.prompt: What should you keep even when AI helps?
options: Every first draft
The longest possible prompt
Your judgment
A secret fear of buttons
questions.answer: Your judgment
questions.explain: AI can draft, summarize, and organize. You still decide what is right, useful, and worth sending.
questions.review: Find it in the Core Lesson.

questions.prompt: What kind of first task belongs in the Episode 1 try-on?
options: A low-risk work explanation or draft you can judge
A confidential legal conclusion
A customer commitment with no review
A company policy you will never check
questions.answer: A low-risk work explanation or draft you can judge
questions.explain: The first try should be useful, small, and safe enough that you can learn without handing it the car keys.
questions.review: Find it in the Episode 1 Fun Pack Try-On.

questions.prompt: Why does the room matter?
options: Because AI works better when lonely
Because no one should ever ask a question publicly
Because learning is easier when women trade questions, receipts, and shortcuts
Because every answer belongs in a private notebook
questions.answer: Because learning is easier when women trade questions, receipts, and shortcuts
questions.explain: The community piece matters because the questions, wins, and messy attempts are useful to more than one person.
questions.review: Find it in the community section and Website Modules.

questions.prompt: Bonus: next week, prompting gets compared to what?
options: A vending machine
Delegating with context
A horoscope with Wi-Fi
A search bar wearing lip gloss
questions.answer: Delegating with context
questions.explain: Episode 2 is about prompting as delegation: task, audience, context, standards, and constraints.
questions.review: Preview Episode 2 when you are ready.

questions.prompt: Bonus: who becomes the patron saint of specificity in Episode 2?
options: David Rose
Ross Geller
The AOL running man
A Furby with boundaries
questions.answer: David Rose
questions.explain: David Rose is the reminder that specific is not fussy. Specific is useful.
questions.review: Preview Episode 2's David Rose section.

issue02.label: Episode 02 Quiz
issue02.optionLabel: Episode 02: Tell Me What You Want
issue02.title: Tell me what you want, but make it painfully specific.
issue02.intro: Answer ten Episode 2 questions, then try the two Burn Book bonus questions. The score is out of 10, but the extra credit girls can still get 12/10.

questions.prompt: What usually happens when you give AI a vague ask?
options: It reads your mind
It gives you vague output
It becomes a VP
It automatically knows your office politics
questions.answer: It gives you vague output
questions.explain: Episode 2 is the Spice Girls lesson: tell it what you want, not what you hope it guesses.
questions.review: Find it in the opening and 'Tell Me What You Want' section.

questions.prompt: Prompting is closer to:
options: Coding from scratch
Manifesting at a laptop
Delegating with context
Typing one magic word
questions.answer: Delegating with context
questions.explain: A good prompt is a brief: task, audience, context, standards, constraints, and what good looks like.
questions.review: Find it in the Episode Promise and David Rose section.

questions.prompt: Why is David Rose useful for prompting?
options: He makes every answer shorter
He replaces judgment
He reminds us to be very specific
He only works for fashion prompts
questions.answer: He reminds us to be very specific
questions.explain: The David Rose move is not being fussy for sport. It is giving enough detail that the output has a chance.
questions.review: Find it in The David Rose School of Prompting.

questions.prompt: What does the drawing-game analogy show?
options: The person drawing can only use the details you give them
AI hates pencils
A vague description always wins
Prompting is mostly about being cute
questions.answer: The person drawing can only use the details you give them
questions.explain: The better the description, the more recognizable the result.
questions.review: Find it in 'Tell Me What You Want, What You Really Really Want.'

questions.prompt: Which detail belongs in a stronger prompt?
options: Only the word 'better'
A complaint about being busy
Nothing, because AI should know
Audience, tone, length, and what not to include
questions.answer: Audience, tone, length, and what not to include
questions.explain: Context is the difference between generic beige output and something you might actually send.
questions.review: Find it in The David Rose School of Prompting.

questions.prompt: What is the 'fold in the cheese' lesson?
options: If your instruction is unclear, AI may try but still miss what you meant
Cheese fixes every prompt
AI should always cook dinner
Short prompts are always better
questions.answer: If your instruction is unclear, AI may try but still miss what you meant
questions.explain: The tool cannot execute the standard you did not explain.
questions.review: Find it in The David Rose School of Prompting.

questions.prompt: If the first AI output is bad, what is the smarter next move?
options: Declare the whole technology useless
Forward it anyway
Improve the ask and try again
Apologize to the laptop
questions.answer: Improve the ask and try again
questions.explain: Bad first output is often feedback on the prompt, not proof that you are doomed.
questions.review: Find it in Same Task, Better Ask.

questions.prompt: Why tell AI what not to include?
options: It makes the answer longer
It deletes all creativity
It sets boundaries before the draft wanders off
It turns the prompt into code
questions.answer: It sets boundaries before the draft wanders off
questions.explain: Constraints are useful. They keep the output from adding fluff, fake confidence, or a tone you would never use.
questions.review: Find it in The David Rose School of Prompting.

questions.prompt: What does the Harvard/BCG research note warn us about?
options: AI always improves everything
AI can help inside its strengths, but polished wrong answers still need judgment
Consultants should stop using tools
Specific prompts do not matter
questions.answer: AI can help inside its strengths, but polished wrong answers still need judgment
questions.explain: The lesson is not blind trust. It is context, judgment, and verification.
questions.review: Find it in the Research Note.

questions.prompt: What was the Episode 2 try-on?
options: Memorize every AI product name
Build an app before lunch
Give AI the same real task twice: once vague, once specific
Ask AI to pick your outfit and call it strategy
questions.answer: Give AI the same real task twice: once vague, once specific
questions.explain: The point is to see the difference. Same task, better brief, much better odds.
questions.review: Find it in the Episode 2 Fun Pack Try-On.

questions.prompt: Bonus: next week's Burn Book episode is about what AI problem?
options: AI hallucinations
Keyboard shortcuts
Newsletter fonts
Spreadsheet tabs
questions.answer: AI hallucinations
questions.explain: Episode 3 is about confident output that may be wrong, unsupported, outdated, or made up.
questions.review: Preview the next Episode once it drops.

questions.prompt: Bonus: what should you ask for before trusting high-stakes AI output?
options: A prettier paragraph
More exclamation marks
Receipts
A glitter filter
questions.answer: Receipts
questions.explain: If the claim matters, the source matters. Confidence is not a citation.
questions.review: Preview the next Episode once it drops.

issue03.label: Episode 03 Quiz
issue03.optionLabel: Episode 03: Don't Be Chutney on the Stand
issue03.title: Don't Be Chutney on the Stand
issue03.intro: Do not be Chutney on the stand. Be Elle with the timeline. Answer ten Episode 3 questions, then try the two bonus questions from next week's locker. The score is out of 10, but the extra credit girls can still get 12/10.

questions.prompt: What is Don't Be Chutney on the Stand in Episode 3?
options: AI is always malicious when it is wrong
AI can make unsupported information look as finished as supported information
AI should only be used for jokes
AI works only when every answer has a pink notebook
questions.answer: AI can make unsupported information look as finished as supported information
questions.explain: The Episode teaches that the same confident format can make real facts, stale facts, assumptions, and made-up claims look equally finished.
questions.review: Find it in Don't Be Chutney on the Stand section.

questions.prompt: What is the key judgment skill this week?
options: Never use AI again
Trust every polished answer
Check the alibi before it gets on the stand
Make the prompt longer no matter what
questions.answer: Check the alibi before it gets on the stand
questions.explain: Episode 3 is not paranoia. It is judgment: use the draft, then verify the claim, timeline, source, or context before you rely on it.
questions.review: Find it in the Episode Promise and opening.

questions.prompt: What does “She doesn’t even go here” mean at work?
options: The answer is formatted badly
The answer may sound plausible but does not match your actual company, customer, market, policy, date, or decision
The answer used too many bullets
The answer is too short to use
questions.answer: The answer may sound plausible but does not match your actual company, customer, market, policy, date, or decision
questions.explain: The line becomes a context check for adjacent-but-wrong output.
questions.review: Find it in She Doesn’t Even Go Here.

questions.prompt: In the Cher's Closet section, how should you sort AI output before using it?
options: Drafts, claims, and receipts
Fonts, colors, and captions
Long answers, short answers, and medium answers
Compliments, caveats, and calendar invites
questions.answer: Drafts, claims, and receipts
questions.explain: Drafts can help with wording and structure. Claims need checking. Receipts are the source, date, quote, number, or record you can point to.
questions.review: Find it in Cher's Closet Can Pick The Outfit. You Check The Dress Code.

questions.prompt: What kind of work can AI usually help with safely as a first pass?
options: Structure, drafts, checklists, plain-language rewrites, and possible gaps
Final legal conclusions with no review
Current pricing without opening the source
Company policy exceptions it has never seen
questions.answer: Structure, drafts, checklists, plain-language rewrites, and possible gaps
questions.explain: Episode 3 says AI can be useful for shaping the work, while exact facts and high-stakes claims still need verification.
questions.review: Find it in Cher's Closet Can Pick The Outfit. You Check The Dress Code.

questions.prompt: Which items should you verify before using AI output at work?
options: Names, dates, numbers, links, quotes, prices, policies, customer commitments, and anything you would defend in a meeting
Only the font and paragraph length
Only whether the answer sounds confident
Nothing if the answer has bullets
questions.answer: Names, dates, numbers, links, quotes, prices, policies, customer commitments, and anything you would defend in a meeting
questions.explain: The receipts habit is about checking the claims that could embarrass you, mislead someone, cost money, or create real risk.
questions.review: Find it in Elle Woods Would Like To See The File and The Receipts Pass Study Montage.

questions.prompt: Why is asking “Are you sure?” again, and again, not enough?
options: Because it asks the same unreliable answer to certify itself
Because it makes the answer too short
Because AI refuses yes-or-no questions
Because it removes all useful structure
questions.answer: Because it asks the same unreliable answer to certify itself
questions.explain: Chutney can repeat the same alibi. Verification means checking the claim against a source, date, quote, number, context, or domain rule.
questions.review: Find it in Chutney Can Say It Thrice. Elle Still Checks The Timeline.

questions.prompt: What should Prompt Like Elle ask AI to separate?
options: Draft language, claims needing receipts, assumptions, fragile details, and the receipt to check
Only the funny sentences
Only the shortest bullets
Only what sounds most executive
questions.answer: Draft language, claims needing receipts, assumptions, fragile details, and the receipt to check
questions.explain: The prompt moves the answer from monologue to testimony: claim over here, source over there, suspicious timeline detail where you can see it.
questions.review: Find it in Chutney Can Say It Thrice. Elle Still Checks The Timeline.

questions.prompt: For legal, HR, finance, privacy, security, or policy-sensitive work, AI should be treated as:
options: The final authority
A helper for preparing questions and organizing facts, not the owner of the answer
A replacement for source review
A shortcut around approval
questions.answer: A helper for preparing questions and organizing facts, not the owner of the answer
questions.explain: The Episode keeps high-stakes work inside human/source review boundaries.
questions.review: Find it in Cher's Closet Can Pick The Outfit. You Check The Dress Code.

questions.prompt: What is the Episode 3 Try-On?
options: Use Prompt Like Elle on a low-risk task, then verify the claims yourself
Ask AI to write a movie review
Use AI output without edits for speed
Compare every AI company in one sitting
questions.answer: Use Prompt Like Elle on a low-risk task, then verify the claims yourself
questions.explain: The Try-On asks readers to open their own AI tool, paste Prompt Like Elle, add a low-risk task or source notes, and then do three human checks: a fact, a context-dependent claim, and a claim you would be embarrassed to say without a receipt.
questions.review: Find it in The Receipts Pass Study Montage.

questions.prompt: Bonus: next week's Boy Band Lineup is about what?
options: Choosing between ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini by strengths and tradeoffs
Using one AI tool for everything forever
Ranking boy bands by frosted tips
Replacing verification with celebrity gossip
questions.answer: Choosing between ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini by strengths and tradeoffs
questions.explain: Episode 4 is the tool-comparison week: same general category, different strengths, different tradeoffs, different reasons to pick the lead singer for the task.
questions.review: Preview Episode 4 once it drops.

questions.prompt: Bonus: in next week's tool comparison, what does choosing the lead singer mean?
options: Picking the tool that best fits the job instead of defaulting to the loudest name
Letting the cutest app icon make the decision
Skipping the brief because the tool is popular
Assuming every AI product works the same way
questions.answer: Picking the tool that best fits the job instead of defaulting to the loudest name
questions.explain: The next move after receipts is agency: you do not need one favorite forever. You need to know which tool belongs on lead vocals for this task.
questions.review: Preview Episode 4 once it drops.

issue04.label: Episode 04 Quiz
issue04.optionLabel: Episode 04: Every SLAiYER Needs a Watcher
issue04.title: Which tool, for which job — and staying the one who decides.
issue04.intro: Answer ten Episode 4 questions from the SLAiYER Handbook, then try the two bonus questions teasing next week's roll call. A perfect 12/10 gets two stickers, because we are not monsters.

questions.prompt: Chapter 1 opens with "Every Slayer needs a Watcher." In that framing, what is the Handbook's job?
options: The Handbook is your Watcher — it tells you what you're walking into before you walk in, while you stay the Slayer doing the work
The Handbook is the Slayer, and you're its sidekick
The Handbook fights your battles for you so you don't have to
The Handbook is just a glossary — no Slayer or Watcher involved
questions.answer: The Handbook is your Watcher — it tells you what you're walking into before you walk in, while you stay the Slayer doing the work
questions.explain: You're always the Slayer — the one who goes out and does the work. The Handbook is the Watcher: it briefs you, names what's in front of you, but never swings for you.
questions.review: Find it in Chapter 1, Every Slayer Needs a Watcher.

questions.prompt: Your colleague says "just use AI for it." What's missing from that sentence?
options: Nothing — that's exactly the right instinct
AI can't really help with work tasks anyway
"AI" isn't one thing — which tool, for which job, is the whole question
You should clear it with IT first
questions.answer: "AI" isn't one thing — which tool, for which job, is the whole question
questions.explain: "Just use AI" lands like "just use internet." The Handbook exists because the useful question is never whether — it's which tool, for which job.
questions.review: Find it in Chapter 1's opening.

questions.prompt: The Field Guide says "graduate to a specialist only when the generalist fails in front of you." Which of these is a real graduate-now moment?
options: The generalist gave you a draft you'd like to tweak a little
You're just curious whether a fancier tool exists
You need live, current sources with links — and the generalist can't actually browse or cite them
The generalist answered, but a coworker prefers a different brand
questions.answer: You need live, current sources with links — and the generalist can't actually browse or cite them
questions.explain: Graduate when the generalist hits a real wall — needs live web sources, a true document tool, image work it can't do. Not because the draft's imperfect, not because something shinier exists. The task tells you, not the marketing.
questions.review: Find it in Chapter 4, The Field Guide.

questions.prompt: Chapter 1's "training data" entry warns that what you type today might train tomorrow's model. For free/personal accounts, what's the usual default?
options: Training is OFF unless you turn it on
Training is often ON by default — your inputs can feed the model
There's no difference between free and paid on this
Only images get used, never text
questions.answer: Training is often ON by default — your inputs can feed the model
questions.explain: Personal/free accounts commonly default to training ON; business-approved accounts default OFF. What you paste can become tomorrow's training set. (Ch 5 turns this into the account rule.)
questions.review: Find it in Chapter 1's Vocabulary, the training-data entry.

questions.prompt: The Skeleton Key (Chapter 3) is the reusable profile that travels across every tool. What three things is it made of?
options: Username, password, payment method
Custom Instructions, Memory, and Projects
Prompts, files, and bookmarks
The paid plan, the app, and the login
questions.answer: Custom Instructions, Memory, and Projects
questions.explain: Custom Instructions (standing orders), Memory (the part that pays attention on its own — but it rots, so check it), Projects (rooms for one job). "One key, every door."
questions.review: Find it in Chapter 3, The Skeleton Key.

questions.prompt: Chapter 4's Field Guide sorts tools into five categories. Where do ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini all sit?
options: Each is its own separate category
They're all "big general assistants" — the same category
They're "specialists"
They're "power tools"
questions.answer: They're all "big general assistants" — the same category
questions.explain: The famous names are all generalists — same category, not rivals in different tiers. Specialists (Perplexity, NotebookLM), visual tools, power tools, and advanced agents are the other four.
questions.review: Find it in Chapter 4, The Field Guide.

questions.prompt: What's the Field Guide's rule for actually picking a tool?
options: Always start with a specialist built for your exact task
Pick whichever your company pays for
Default to the generalist; graduate to a specialist only when it fails in front of you
Try all five categories and compare every time
questions.answer: Default to the generalist; graduate to a specialist only when it fails in front of you
questions.explain: Start with the generalist. Reach for a specialist only when the generalist visibly falls short on the real task — not before. Match the type to the job and the right tool falls out.
questions.review: Find it in Chapter 4, The Field Guide.

questions.prompt: Chapter 1 says to be "a Watcher, not a believer." When the tool hands you a confident answer, what does that mean you do?
options: Trust it — confidence means it checked its work
Reject everything it says and do it yourself anyway
Take it as a lead to verify, not a verdict to accept — you stay the one who decides what's true
Only double-check if it actually sounds unsure
questions.answer: Take it as a lead to verify, not a verdict to accept — you stay the one who decides what's true
questions.explain: A Watcher doesn't take the tool's word — she reads what it brings back with her eyes open. Confident ≠ correct. You direct and you verify; the tool advises.
questions.review: Find it in Chapter 1, be a Watcher, not a believer.

questions.prompt: Chapter 5's Account Rule is the data-safety rule. What's its core warning about free tools at work?
options: Free tools are always fine for anything
Free tools are just slower, that's the only downside
"When the tool is free, the product is you" — use the company-approved account for work data
You should personally pay for every tool you use
questions.answer: "When the tool is free, the product is you" — use the company-approved account for work data
questions.explain: Free/personal accounts can turn your work data into someone's training set. Use the approved account. Read the box. Don't be Deb.
questions.review: Find it in Chapter 5, The Account Rule.

questions.prompt: The Account Rule closes on the difference between "I wasn't sure, so I asked" and "I figured it was probably fine." What does "approved" actually mean?
options: The tool has good reviews online
Lots of your coworkers already use it
A person with the authority to decide looked at this exact tool and said yes
It's free, so there's nothing to approve
questions.answer: A person with the authority to decide looked at this exact tool and said yes
questions.explain: "Approved means a human with the authority to decide looked at this exact tool and said yes." Not vibes, not popularity — an actual yes from someone who can give it. The one Deb skips.
questions.review: Find it in Chapter 5, The Account Rule.
